newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaireans in capital wait for rebels with open arms.
newsitem.headline: Zaireans in capital wait for rebels with open arms.

text.p: Zaireans in the capital Kinshasa say they would welcome rebel leader Laurent Kabila with open arms but their hopes of a better future under new rule are tinged with fears of the storm that may precede him.
In the dusty and crowded streets of Kasa-Vubu suburb in the tense capital of five million people, support for President Mobutu Sese Seko, ruler of 31 years, seems to have dried up.
"Here in Kinshasa 95 percent of the people are waiting for Kabila with open arms," said Jean Matadi, a Zairean aged 49.
"We wanted Kabila to take Kisangani and now we want him to take the country. He is a dynamic man who has managed to put Mobutu to flight," said Filo Nkomba, 37, a civil servant.
"He is a son of the country," said Theo Nduli, who repairs tyres and charges car batteries to try to make ends meet.
Locals say corruption turned all but a chosen few into paupers in a country rich with gold, minerals and fertile soils.
State news broadcasts ignored Saturday's fall of Zaire's third city Kisangani in favour of reports on the problem of female circumcision and a school teacher's sex scandal.
But everyone in town knows about the latest rebel victory.
Kisangani's fall is the greatest physical and psychological blow to government attempts to counter a five-month insurrection that ethnic Tutsis near the Rwandan border began.
"It's finished for Mobutu," Nduli said. "We need Kabila."
Some people have high hopes of a peaceful transition in the capital. Others feared bloodshed with Kabila coming to settle scores, or before then among rivals for power or army control.
Opposition to Mobutu, who seized power in 1965, has always found fertile ground in Kinshasa.
Mobutu, 66, bowed to pressure for democratic change in 1990 but the transition has dragged. He has spent most of his time in Europe since cancer surgery in August.
Many Kinshasans say his time has passed.

A March poll in the city showed just over half had a good opinion of Kabila. A mere 13 percent had a good opinion of Mobutu. Etienne Tshisekedi, another veteran Mobutu opponent, remains highly popular.
"We are no longer afraid of Mobutu. For the first time, an end is in sight," Nduli said over a beer in Ma Nelly's cafe.
Jubilant crowds greeted Mobutu in Kinshasa when he returned home in December, hoping he would resolve the crisis.
Since then, Kabila's alliance of several opposition forces has taken a fifth of the country. Resistance from the rag-tag and barely paid national army has collapsed along the way.
Kabila says he will march on Kinshasa unless Mobutu talks to him face-to-face but distances are vast and roads abysmal so this route could take him weeks -- even unopposed.
"Only the Lord knows when he will come, but come he will, and when we see him we will applaud him," said Nkomba. "But if Mobutu comes back (from France), we'll stone him."
Many in Kinshasa fear a coup or general chaos before Kabila arrives. Zairean troops have a reputation for rampaging and looting as they flee. They looted Kinshasa in the early 1990s.
"Part of the army supports the people and part Mobutu. The people's army will put down its arms, and if the army of Mobutu resists, they can fight it out together," said Matadi.
"Maybe there'll be some looting but well, we're used to that, our army's always doing it. Anyway, it will only last a couple of days."
